title: The Living God and the Scarecrow Gods
summary: Jeremiah mocks the idols of the nations as carved wood covered in metal and cloth, things that must be carried because they cannot walk, and sets against them the LORD who made the earth and rules the storm. The chapter then turns to Judah: pack your bundle, for the siege is coming. It closes with a lament over a ruined tent and a prayer that God would correct his people with justice rather than anger.
story: Chapters 7 to 10 gather Jeremiah's preaching against a false confidence: trust in the temple building, in ritual, in wisdom and wealth. Chapter 10 reaches the root of that confidence, which is the question of which God Judah actually trusts. The people had spent generations adding the gods of their neighbors to the worship of the LORD, and the prophets called that betrayal. Here Jeremiah answers it with ridicule and with praise. The second half of the chapter pulls back from the nations to the city itself, where the army from the north is already on the road, and it ends with the first clear sound of a voice that will grow louder in chapters 11 to 20: the prophet, or the city he speaks for, crying out in pain and asking God for mercy within judgment.
historical:
Jeremiah preached in Jerusalem from about 627 BC, the thirteenth year of King Josiah (1:2), until after the city fell to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC. Much of chapters 7 to 20 is usually placed in the reign of Jehoiakim (609 to 598 BC), when Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar had replaced Assyria and Egypt as the power pressing on Judah. The warning of a report from “the land to the north” (verse 22) fits that setting, since Babylon's armies came down into Judah along the northern route through Syria. The command to gather belongings “you who live under siege” (verse 17) looks ahead to the sieges of 597 and 588 to 586 BC.

The chapter also has a textual history worth knowing. The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament made by Jewish scholars in the last centuries BC) has a Jeremiah about one-seventh shorter than the traditional Hebrew text, and in this chapter it lacks verses 6 to 8 and 10, the hymns of praise, and places verse 9 inside verse 5. A Hebrew fragment of Jeremiah found at Qumran agrees with the shorter form here. Many scholars conclude that two editions of the book circulated. The praise the longer text includes is fully at home in Jeremiah's thought either way.
cultural:
The idol-making described in verses 3 to 5 and 9 matches what we know of ancient Near Eastern practice. A statue of a god often had a wooden core, overlaid with beaten silver and gold, fixed firmly on its base, and dressed in fine garments dyed blue and purple. Purple dye came from sea snails harvested on the Phoenician coast and was among the costliest goods of the ancient world. Tarshish was a distant western port known for trade in metals (its location is debated, with southern Spain the most common suggestion), and Uphaz is unknown; some interpreters think it is another spelling of Ophir, the famous source of gold. In Mesopotamia, a finished statue went through rites that were believed to open its mouth and make it a dwelling for the god. Idols were also carried in public procession on festival days, which gives bite to the jibe that “They must be carried because they cannot walk.”

The “signs in the heavens” in verse 2 point to astrology and the reading of omens in eclipses, comets, and planetary movements, a sophisticated science in Babylon that royal courts took very seriously. Jeremiah does not deny that the nations were afraid of these signs. He says Israel need not be, because the one who made the heavens is not bound by them. Verse 11 is written in Aramaic, not Hebrew, the only such verse in the book. Aramaic was the common language of diplomacy and trade across the empires, so the line reads like a message Israel is given to say in the nations' own tongue.
literary: Verses 1 to 16 alternate between satire and hymn. Each stretch of mockery (verses 2 to 5, 8 to 9, 14 to 15) is answered by praise (verses 6 to 7, 10, 12 to 13, 16), so the reader keeps swinging between the lifeless thing and the living God. The satire uses the vocabulary of craft (chisel, hammer, nails, goldsmith), while the praise uses the vocabulary of creation (power, wisdom, understanding, thunder, wind). Verses 12 to 16 appear again almost word for word in 51:15-19. The chapter then shifts to a poem of coming siege (verses 17 to 22), a lament in the first person in which the speaker's tent is torn down and his sons are gone, and a closing prayer (verses 23 to 25) whose last verse closely parallels Psalm 79:6-7. Whether the lamenting voice in verses 19 and 20 is Jeremiah himself or Jerusalem personified as a mother who has lost her children is debated; the imagery allows both, and the prophet often speaks from inside his people's grief.

outline.t: Do not fear the signs or the scarecrow gods
There is none like the LORD, the living God
The gods who made nothing, and the Maker of all
Gather your bundle: the siege is coming
A prayer for correction with justice

doctrines.note: The chapter's argument against idols is not only that they are false but that they are made: a creature cannot save the one who made it. Whatever we must carry, protect, and polish in order to keep it standing cannot carry us.

The LORD is “the Maker of all things” (verse 16), who made the earth by his power and wisdom and commands the weather. Because he made the heavens, the signs in them hold no authority over his people.
He is called “the true God”, “the living God and eternal King”, and “King of nations”. The chapter's confession is that the LORD is not Israel's tribal god alone but the ruler of every people.

The closing prayer accepts that God's discipline is deserved, yet asks for correction “only with justice” and “not in Your anger”. Judgment in Jeremiah always aims at a people who can still be restored.

words.note: Hevel, breath or vapor, translated here as worthless (verses 3, 8, and 15). It is the same word that runs through Ecclesiastes as vanity or meaninglessness. Applied to idols, it means they have no substance at all: something as empty as your breath on a cold day. Jeremiah uses it for the gods Israel chased (2:5), and the irony is sharp, since in verse 14 the idols have “no breath in them” of any other kind.

Cheleq, portion or share, as in a share of land or an inheritance. “The Portion of Jacob” in verse 16 is God himself: where other peoples had idols as their allotted gods, Israel's allotment was the LORD. The word appears in the Psalms in the same sense (the LORD is my portion), and here it is paired with Israel as “the tribe of His inheritance”, so the belonging runs in both directions.

Yasar, to discipline, correct, or instruct, the way a parent trains a child. In verse 24 the speaker does not ask to escape correction but to receive it with justice. The related noun musar appears in verse 8, where the nations are “instructed by worthless idols”, so the chapter contrasts two teachers: dead wood and the living God.

christ: The New Testament picks up this chapter's contrast between dead idols and the living God. Paul praises the Thessalonians for turning to God from idols to serve the living and true God (1 Thessalonians 1:9), and in Lystra and Athens he calls people away from worthless things to the God who made heaven and earth and does not live in shrines made by hands (Acts 14:15; 17:24-25). The deeper link is thematic: idols are carried, but the God of Israel carries his people, a contrast Isaiah draws explicitly (Isaiah 46:1-4). In Jesus that God comes to carry the weight himself. The prayer of verse 24, correction with justice and not destruction, finds its answer in a cross where judgment falls and a people is not brought to nothing.

hard.q: Isn't it unfair to mock other people's religion as nothing but wood and metal?
hard.a: The satire can sound crude to modern ears, and ancient worshipers did not think the statue was the god in a simple way; they believed a deity could come to dwell in a properly consecrated image. Jeremiah likely knew that. His point is that whatever the theory, the practice ended in people bowing before an object their own hands had made, and fearing powers that could not act. The chapter is also addressed first to Israel, not to outsiders (verse 1): its target is God's own people borrowing a religion they had been warned against, and it is an internal warning before it is an attack on anyone else. Christians reading it today have generally applied it not only to statues but to anything they build and then trust to save them.

questions: The idols had to be nailed down so they would not topple. What do you find yourself propping up, protecting, or maintaining because you depend on it for security?
The nations were terrified by signs in the heavens. What omens, forecasts, or headlines make you afraid, and how does verse 12 speak to that fear?
Verse 24 asks for correction with justice rather than no correction at all. What would it mean to ask God for that kind of discipline in your own life?
